title.narrative: Integrated climate risk management for strengthened resilience to climate change in Buner and Shangla Districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Province, Pakistan

description.narrative:
16. To meet the project’s overarching objective, three Components are proposed. Under Component 1, the project will improve forecasting and early warning capacity and implement prioritized anticipatory actions that are designed to mitigate the impacts of flooding. Under Component 2, the project will support communities to develop adaptation plans and implement priority adaptation actions, as well as have access to sustainable sources of financial and technical support. Activities under Component 1 will deliver benefits in terms of reduced impacts from floods in the shorter term, while activities under Component 2 will support vulnerable people to adapt to projected changes in flooding frequency and severity in the longer term. Component 3 will then bring together knowledge and co-learning from the project and aims to support replication and integration with financing mechanisms at the provincial and national level.
Component 1: Improved capacity for flood forecasting, early warning systems, and anticipatory actions in Buner and Shangla Districts
17. The early warning system will be enhanced at the district level in Shangla and Buner in close collaboration with national and provincial level government partners and institutes. The primary stakeholders will be the Planning and Development Department, as Executing Entity, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Provincial Disaster Management Agency (PDMA) and its counterparts at the National and District Levels, the PMD, and the Flood Forecasting Division (FFD).[1] [https://wfp.sharepoint.com/sites/OSZIR949/Shared%20Documents/Climate%20Finance/2.%20Green%20Climate%20Fund%20(GCF)/2.%20Projects/Pakistan%20GCF/Concept%20note/Resubmission%20August%202021/GCF%20WFP%20Concept%20Note%20clean%2025%20August%202021%20for%20resubmission.docx#_ftn1] The project will improve both the weather information sharing environment through enhanced vertical and horizontal coordination and knowledge flows, and the flood early-warning system, which will be used to design and implement anticipatory actions against a potential flood in the target districts. As part of the activities under Component 1, WFP, along with its national and provincial government partners, and local stakeholders, will determine the appropriate early warning triggers, thresholds and anticipatory actions, so that timely and effective anticipatory actions can be implemented at the community level.
The following outputs and indicative activities are proposed under Component 1:
Output 1.1 – Flood Forecasting capability strengthened.
18. Interviews and consultations with PDMA, PMD, FFD and the Ministry of Climate Change at the national level highlighted the lack of hydrometeorological stations in the target districts and a lack of human resource capacity. Each department requested capacity-building support in areas relating to hydro-meteorological monitoring equipment, human resource capacity and early warning systems (addressed under Output 1.2). Given the size of the target area, its topography and remoteness a full assessment with regard to existing capacity gaps and hydro-meteorological station needs will be carried out during the full proposal development stage, with a specific focus on: (a) Review the PMD/FFD flood forecasting institutional and human resource capacity and services provided to Shangla and Buner Districts; (b) Assess hydro-meteorological station needs in Shangla and Buner districts. The assessment will allow to clearly identify activities that are needed to strengthen flood forecasting capacities, which can be indicatively summarized as: 1) build short-range and seasonal flood-forecasting capacity at PMD/FFD and at the Regional Meteorological Centre, Peshawar; and 2) procure and install hydro-meteorological stations in the target districts, based on the assessments undertaken during FP development. The activities proposed under this output will be further unpacked and clarified during FP development.
Output 1.2 – Early Warning System strengthened in the two target districts.
19. Indicative activities: 1) Strengthen governance structures to effectively develop and coordinate EWS implementation in the two districts. This includes building capacity of the District Disaster Management Authority (DDMA), supporting the government to re-constitute disaster management committees and developing procedures and protocols. This activity is included to respond to needs identified in consultation with PDMA and the P&D Department, which highlighted that the Disaster Management Committees exist but lack capacity, a formal mandate, and operating protocols and procedures. As a result, the lack of coordination on the EWS leads to serious delays in providing timely warning, 2) Review the current EWS in Shangla and Buner Districts to establish areas for strengthening and improve government capacity to reach the most vulnerable people with EWS, 3) Implement improvements to the early warning system in the target districts based on the review conducted in activity 1.2.2, 4) Develop a communication strategy and protocol for the dissemination of early warning messages for vulnerable communities.
Output 1.3 – Strengthened capacity of provincial government to implement anticipatory actions.
20. Indicative activities: 1) Assess the potential of existing national and provincial systems to deliver anticipatory actions at scale; 2) Develop impact-based flood-forecast triggers and thresholds in flood-affected areas of Shangla and Buner Districts; 3) Define anticipatory action SOPs at the district and community levels which include triggers, thresholds, anticipatory actions, finance, targeting, and implementation stakeholders; 4) Formulate technical working groups to validate anticipatory action SOPs and support the integration into district and community disaster risk management policy, plans and budgets; 5) Work with government social protection systems (such as BISP) to link database of poor households and aid-delivery mechanisms with a forecast-based financing system for anticipatory actions.
Output 1.4 - Anticipatory actions implemented in the two target districts to effectively mitigate and manage flood risks.
21. Indicative activities: 1) Implement the anticipatory actions according to the SOPs and implementation structures developed through activities under Output 1.3.
22. Output 1.4 will use the project funding for anticipatory action to support vulnerable populations in the event of of a forecast trigger being activated to reduce any potential damage and losses and mitigate potential impacts through activities undertaken before. Based on the local context and preparatory work under
Outputs 1.1-1.3, assistance will be channelled through existing WFP and government delivery systems in alignment with the anticipatory action SOPs. Anticipatory actions that can yield high impacts at household level and that can be operationally delivered at scale will be prioritised. Potential examples include expanding the registry of people who receive social protection/cash transfers to enable them to receive funds to use for resilience building/anticipatory action before a flooding event, improved crop/livestock storage to protect these from rising waters and the preparation of emergency food parcels. amongst others. The exact nature of anticipatory actions will be detailed through activities under Outputs 1.1-1.3, further work to specify the nature of the actions will be carried out at the funding proposal development stage. WFP’s experience in other settings shows that anticipatory assistance to affected people considerably reduced potential loss and damages from extreme weather events[2] [https://wfp.sharepoint.com/sites/OSZIR949/Shared%20Documents/Climate%20Finance/2.%20Green%20Climate%20Fund%20(GCF)/2.%20Projects/Pakistan%20GCF/Concept%20note/Resubmission%20August%202021/GCF%20WFP%20Concept%20Note%20clean%2025%20August%202021%20for%20resubmission.docx#_ftn2] Note that activities under Outputs 1.3 and 1.4 differ from emergency response because they are designed to put in place procedures to increase the ability to reduce potential impacts, withstand and recover from increasingly frequent and severe floods in the target districts.
Component 2: Increased climate resilience through local adaptation plans, diversified livelihoods, and sustainable finance
23. Increasing temperatures and changing weather systems are impacting the water and agriculture sectors. Agriculture and livestock, as the main sources of livelihood in the target districts, are being directly affected. As crop yield suffers due to different stressors, particularly floods, food insecurity increases, and livelihoods are threatened. There is a need to support the local communities in developing their capacity to adapt and become more resilient to the changing climate. As previously highlighted, low levels of literacy – especially among women – and limited, non-climate responsive social protection has further increased community vulnerability. Most families in Buner and Shangla rely on a single livelihood source, which leaves them vulnerable to a total loss of income.
24. Component 2 will strengthen adaptation planning and livelihoods at the community level in Buner and Shangla Districts by increasing and diversifying incomes and reducing dependency on flood-affected crops. Under Component 2, community level climate change action plans will be developed and their priority actions implemented. Project interventions will ensure that locally adapted measures for sustainability are in place and the communities are in a position to be able to independently manage their livelihoods in the future. Communities targeted by Component 2 will have benefitted from the improved EWS, forecasting capabilities and anticipatory action SOPs developed in Component 1. However, to adapt to the risk of increasingly frequent and severe flooding in the longer term, communities also require support to plan and implement actions that make their livelihoods more diversified and climate resilient in the longer term.
25. Under Component 2, the following outputs and indicative actions are proposed:
Output 2.1 –Local adaptation plans developed in the target communities in Buner and Shangla.
26. Indicative activities: 1) Building on a climate change analysis performed by WFP, the project will downscale expected impacts to provide an in depth understanding of climate change impacts in the target districts, particularly relating to livelihoods, food security, nutrition, while looking at differentiated impacts by women and men. This information will be presented to local authorities to support its integration in local adaptation plans and strategies. 2) Strengthen understanding of communities of expected impacts from climate change on their livelihoods and support the development of community-adaptation plans in Buner and Shangla through a participatory process, with an emphasis on the specific vulnerabilities and challenges faced by women and other vulnerable groups in the communities.
Output 2.2 – Community prioritized adaptation actions implemented.
27. Specific activities will be determined through the local adaptation planning process. However, these actions will relate to livelihoods and food security and will have minimal operational, environmental and social risks. Indicative actions could include diversified livelihoods, establishment of fruit plantations and nurseries, improved soil conservation and management, improved watershed management, improved water storage (recognizing that access to clean drinking water is often problematic during flood periods), rehabilitating land, micro-scale infrastructure. This micro-scale infrastructure could include small structures to prevent flooding such as small-scale walls or dams. Compliance with Category C/minimum risk requirements under the GCF Environmental and Social Policy and the WFP ESS framework will be an essential prerequisite for the selection of any infrastructure. Before implementing any activities in the field, WFP will conduct a participatory needs assessment at community level that will help to identify required and feasible activities. This assessment will be in line with the WFP Environmental and Social Safeguards risk screening tool, government plans, community needs, feasibility and context. This participatory process will ensure that all project activities are demand driven. The activities will also recognize the differentiated impacts on and roles of men and women, and there will be activities that focus on women’s adaptation actions.
Output 2.3 – Structures in place to enable sustainable community access to financial and technical resources[5] [https://wfp.sharepoint.com/sites/OSZIR949/Shared%20Documents/Climate%20Finance/2.%20Green%20Climate%20Fund%20(GCF)/2.%20Projects/Pakistan%20GCF/Concept%20note/Resubmission%20August%202021/GCF%20WFP%20Concept%20Note%20clean%2025%20August%202021%20for%20resubmission.docx#_ftn5].
28. Indicative activities: 1) Assess provincial and national funding mechanisms available to support the implementation of adaptation actions, with a view to connecting the target communities with domestic public finance from provincial and national sources. The Funding Proposal will establish further target funding sources. This could be linked to social protection (e.g., through BISP) or through other on-budget sources. All indicative activities will pay particular attention to the challenges faced by women and will ensure that the particular needs of women in Buner and Shangla are understood and addressed. 2) Develop a community financial sustainability strategy. This would detail how communities can a) organize their own financial resources (through savings schemes) and b) how they can work with government at the district or provincial level to access funds for adaptation actions in the future; 3) Develop local and provincial capacity to plan and develop community savings, revolving funds and micro-finance products to enable investment in small-scale adaptation actions such as different crop varieties better suited to a changing climate. Access to financial assets such as savings and revolving funds, will enable the communities to be more resilient, plan for and adopt small-scale adaptation actions. This financial element of the project will strengthen its sustainability and build long-term resilience for the communities.
Component 3 – Improved knowledge and increased potential for replication and sustainable finance at the national and provincial level
Output 3.1: Knowledge captured and shared at the provincial and national level to facilitate replication and upscaling.
29. Indicative activities include holding national and-provincial level workshops, developing case studies, activities to transfer knowledge to other flood prone areas, creating linkages back to national level policy and decision-making including through publication and dissemination of knowledge products and policy recommendations that will facilitate dissemination and replication throughout the country, and building integration between national and provincial public finance mechanisms and early warning systems, anticipatory action and adaptation. This output will capture knowledge and best practices from both Components of the project with the aim of enhancing knowledge and potential for replication at the provincial and national level. Particular emphasis will be placed on knowledge and policy recommendations that benefit women.
30. A gender sensitive approach that empowers women and enables them to be agents of positive change will be used throughout the project, building on good practices and lessons from WFP-Government of Pakistan projects in other provinces, where Women’s Community Organizations (WCOs) were created and women engaged in specific activities (e.g. nursery raising, kitchen gardening, livestock management, fuelwood plantation, afforestation, establishment and running of micro-enterprises) and independently took decisions about their priority needs, and selection of activities.
31. Project scalability and potential for transformation. Activities under Component 2 have been tested in small-scale interventions in the framework of early recovery, reconstruction and rehabilitation projects funded through bilateral cooperation. Pakistan’s security situation has improved substantially in recent years, allowing these interventions to be scaled-up to improve the resilience of people in other parts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The forecast-based anticipatory action part of Component 1 will build on recent pilot activities in this direction carried out by the government and other partners, such as UNDP under its GLOF2 project. Forecast-based anticipatory action builds on the framework of a traditional early warning system, by building and strengthening the necessary components to define activities that can be initiated or scaled-up before the impacts of a natural hazard occurs and therefore building people’s capacity to prepare for those impacts.
32. Once the system and structures are in place in Buner and Shangla Districts, forecast-based anticipatory action can be replicated in other areas of Pakistan and applied to other hazards through the support provided under Component 3. With increased knowledge and capacities, district and provincial-level government officials will be able to include anticipatory action approaches, climate change considerations and climate change adaptation activities in other locations’ plans and enable other countries to adapt based on the results of this project. This approach increases the project’s potential for scalability and potential for transformation.
33. Implementation and execution arrangements WFP will act as the GCF Accredited Entity for this project and as Executing Entity (EE) together with the Planning & Development (P&D) department of the Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Province. WFP Pakistan has a strong field presence with field offices and cooperating partners throughout Pakistan, including a WFP sub-office in Peshawar. These executing arrangements have been discussed on numerous occasions ahead of the submission of this concept note with the Planning and Development Department of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Government, the Ministry of Climate Change and other stakeholders at provincial and national level. The execution arrangements will be revisited at the funding proposal stage, based on additional consultations and on an analysis of the Planning and Development Department’s operational and financial management capacity to execute the project. Partnerships with other agencies at the provincial level, including the Regional Meteorological Centre Peshawar, the Provincial Disaster Management Agency and the Flood Forecasting Division will be explored when developing the funding proposal.
34. WFP will sign a subsidiary agreement with the Planning and Development Department of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Province. At the national/policy level, the project will be overseen by a Project Steering Committee, chaired by the Ministry of Climate Change (as the National Designated Authority to the Green Climate Fund), and co-chaired by WFP, the P&D Department of the Government of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, with membership from key stakeholders from the Government of Pakistan (GoP), the National Rural Support Programme and JS Bank (as GCF Direct Access Entities) as well as representatives of the beneficiary communities. Representatives of UNDP, who are implementing the GCF-funded GLOF project, and UNEP, who are providing National Adaptation Planning Support, will be invited to the Project Steering Committee as observers. At the provincial/operational level, this structure will be supported at the technical level by an Advisory Committee that will meet regularly to advise the project implementation and strengthen horizontal and vertical coordination.
A Project Management Unit will be set up and will sit in Peshawar (the Capital of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Province). The PMU will be headed by a Project Manager contracted by WFP and comprising staff and consultants from WFP and the Planning and Development Department of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.
35. Financial and operational risks and mitigation measures.
At present the security situation in Buner and Shangla is good, and no additional or burdensome security precautions are required for WFP or its cooperating partners to enter the project’s target areas. WFP works with the UN Department of Safety and Security in Pakistan to ensure the safety of its staff and operations throughout the country. The security situation will be continuously monitored throughout the project and if it deteriorates alternative operational modalities will be established.
36. The 2020 COVID-19 pandemic is currently an impediment to regular operations in Pakistan, as in many countries. This means that physical gatherings (such as meetings and consultations) have either not been possible, or had to be reduced in scope. However, as the earliest realistic start date for the proposed project is 2022, WFP anticipates some return to normality by then. If pandemic-related restrictions are still in place, WFP and its partners in the government have made good use of digital connectivity so far and will continue to communicate this way. When contacts with communities are required, WFP and the P&D Department can leverage good relationships with cooperating partners[6] [https://wfp.sharepoint.com/sites/OSZIR949/Shared%20Documents/Climate%20Finance/2.%20Green%20Climate%20Fund%20(GCF)/2.%20Projects/Pakistan%20GCF/Concept%20note/Resubmission%20August%202021/GCF%20WFP%20Concept%20Note%20clean%2025%20August%202021%20for%20resubmission.docx#_ftn6] that are embedded in the communities to liaise with them. If restrictions relating to COVID-19 are still in place in 2022, the project will make use of alternative approaches. Consultations in preparation for the CLEAR assessment, for example, can be implemented using a mix of digital and paper-based surveys, and initial consultations with communities can take place outdoors, and/or through intermediaries embedded at the community level. Internet connectivity is strong enough in Pakistan to allow stable communications between WFP’s Country Office in Islamabad and Provincial Government stakeholders based in Peshawar. This approach can also be used to implement community-level activities under Components 1&2.
37. The financial management capacity of the proposed executing partner (the Planning and Development Department) will be comprehensively assessed at the funding proposal stage. However, given that the department has worked with implementing organizations in the past in multilateral climate finance projects (such as UNDP and the National Rural Support Programme), it is likely that the department will have sufficient capacity to execute the project. Political preferences have a small chance of affecting the project. However, no political faction in Pakistan disputes the seriousness or urgency of the climate change-related hazards facing vulnerable districts like Buner and Shangla, and the priorities set out in the Climate Change Policy and associated Action Plan of the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Government are unlikely to change.

[2] [https://wfp.sharepoint.com/sites/OSZIR949/Shared%20Documents/Climate%20Finance/2.%20Green%20Climate%20Fund%20(GCF)/2.%20Projects/Pakistan%20GCF/Concept%20note/Resubmission%20August%202021/GCF%20WFP%20Concept%20Note%20clean%2025%20August%202021%20for%20resubmission.docx#_ftnref2] See for example Pople, A, et al (2021) Anticipatory Cash Transfers in Climate Disaster Response. This study shows that in a flood-prone context in Bangladesh, anticipatory actions of the type proposed here meant people were 36% more likely to go a day without food or water.
[3] [https://wfp.sharepoint.com/sites/OSZIR949/Shared%20Documents/Climate%20Finance/2.%20Green%20Climate%20Fund%20(GCF)/2.%20Projects/Pakistan%20GCF/Concept%20note/Resubmission%20August%202021/GCF%20WFP%20Concept%20Note%20clean%2025%20August%202021%20for%20resubmission.docx#_ftnref3] https://www.wfp.org/publications/2017-clear-approach. The Consolidated Livelihood Exercise for Analyzing Resilience (CLEAR) is an analytical approach developed by WFP to better understand how food security is affected by climate change impacts. Impacts include those related to extreme weather events (such as droughts, floods and cyclones) and to long-term gradual changes (such as shifting rainfall patterns, rising temperatures, increased pests and diseases). In the Asia-Pacific region, CLEAR analyses have been conducted in Afghanistan, Cambodia, Laos, Nepal, Sri Lanka and Timor Leste to date.
[4] [https://wfp.sharepoint.com/sites/OSZIR949/Shared%20Documents/Climate%20Finance/2.%20Green%20Climate%20Fund%20(GCF)/2.%20Projects/Pakistan%20GCF/Concept%20note/Resubmission%20August%202021/GCF%20WFP%20Concept%20Note%20clean%2025%20August%202021%20for%20resubmission.docx#_ftnref4] This publication https://documents.wfp.org/stellent/groups/public/documents/communications/wfp291243.pdf - highlights where CLEAR has been used to inform various adaptation programming. In Cambodia, for example, the CLEAR analysis led directly to adaptation actions that increased food security in a flood-prone area. See Chapter 3 of the publication (from p.25). In Sri Lanka CLEAR was used to the National Adaptation Plan (NAP) developed by the government.
[5] [https://wfp.sharepoint.com/sites/OSZIR949/Shared%20Documents/Climate%20Finance/2.%20Green%20Climate%20Fund%20(GCF)/2.%20Projects/Pakistan%20GCF/Concept%20note/Resubmission%20August%202021/GCF%20WFP%20Concept%20Note%20clean%2025%20August%202021%20for%20resubmission.docx#_ftnref5] Please note that GCF funds will not be used as capital for such mechanisms, but rather to enable their establishment including capacity development, strengthening linkages with existing funding mechanisms among others.
